title: Hannah's prayer (1 Samuel 1–2)
hook: a woman prays so hard the priest thinks she's drunk, then sings like Mary will

segments.voice: Yesterday, gleaning: Boaz telling his workers to drop grain on purpose for Ruth. Your line was kindness on purpose. What did you leave for someone? Day three hundred ninety-seven.

Every year a family travels up to the sanctuary at Shiloh, and every year it's the worst week of the year for one of them. Her name is Hannah, Anna in the Douay-Rheims. Her husband loves her, but she has no children, and his other wife has many, and that other wife needles her about it, year after year, until Hannah can't eat. Her husband tries to help: Am I not better to thee than ten children? It doesn't help. So one year, after the meal, she gets up, goes to the doorway of the house of the Lord, and starts to pray. An old priest named Eli is sitting there on a stool, watching.
screen: `THE YEARLY TRIP TO SHILOH.` → `NO CHILDREN, AND A RIVAL'S TAUNTS.` → `AN OLD PRIEST ON A STOOL, WATCHING.`

segments.voice: Hannah prays with tears. Her lips move, but no sound comes out. In those days people usually prayed aloud, so to Eli this looks like one thing: she's drunk. He tells her to go sleep it off. And she answers him, in the Douay: "I am an exceeding unhappy woman, and have drunk neither wine nor any strong drink, but I have poured out my soul before the Lord." Poured out. Not a polite request. Everything in her, emptied out in front of God. And Eli, to his credit, changes his tune: go in peace, he says, and may God grant your petition. Then a small detail: after that, the text says, her face was no longer sad. Nothing has happened yet. She simply prayed and was heard. Then she has a son, Samuel, and when he's weaned she brings him back to Shiloh and gives him to the Lord's service, just as she vowed. And she sings. Her song begins: "My heart hath rejoiced in the Lord." And it turns the world upside down: the mighty are broken, the weak are girded with strength, the hungry are filled, and God lifts the poor from the dust to sit with princes. If that sounds familiar, it should. Centuries later, a young woman named Mary visits her cousin and sings: my soul doth magnify the Lord, he hath put down the mighty and exalted the humble, filled the hungry with good things. The Church has long heard Hannah's song as the older sister of Mary's Magnificat, and prays it among the Old Testament canticles in the Liturgy of the Hours.
screen: `LIPS MOVING, NO SOUND.` · `I HAVE POURED OUT MY SOUL.` · `HER FACE WAS NO MORE SAD.` · `A SONG THAT MARY WILL ECHO.` · then, large: `MY HEART HATH REJOICED IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pour out one honest prayer. Settle, and breathe. Think of the thing you've been carrying the longest, the ache you don't bring up anymore because people are tired of hearing it, or you are. Don't tidy it. If you pray, tell God exactly how it is, silently, the way Hannah did, lips moving if you like, with no polite words in front. If you don't pray, say it plainly to yourself, all of it, and let it be heard. Then just stay a moment, and notice your face. The bell holds the time.
Hannah's prayer. A silent, tearful prayer at Shiloh, so intense the priest thought she was drunk, and later a song of joy that Mary's Magnificat echoes. Today's word.
Your line: she poured out her soul. Today, when someone tells you something raw, believe them before you judge them, the way Eli finally did. Day three hundred ninety-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Hannah's song as one of the Old Testament canticles in the Liturgy of the Hours, at Morning Prayer, and many couples hoping for a child find company in her story.

fork.setup: you're Hannah. you've prayed your heart out in silence, and the priest accuses you of being drunk. what do you do?
options: leave in shame without a word.
tell him the truth: you've poured out your soul before the Lord.
argue with him and storm off.
fork.reveal: she answers him honestly, and Eli blesses her: go in peace. a priest learns to read a broken heart, and she leaves no longer sad.

original.note: Hebrew: Hannah, a name related to the word for grace or favor. The Latin and the Douay call her Anna.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad woman asks for a baby and gets one.
what it means: a woman pours out her soul so fully the priest misreads it, is heard, and sings a song where God lifts the poor and humbles the proud.
what a scholar hears: Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2 is closely echoed in Mary's Magnificat in Luke 1, and the Church prays both.

notes: The Douay-Rheims names 1 Samuel as 1 Kings; refs give both.
'In those days people usually prayed aloud' is a common explanation of Eli's mistake; confirm or soften.
The Magnificat is paraphrased, not quoted; 'my soul doth magnify the Lord' is spoken without quotation marks. Confirm.
Hannah's canticle (1 Samuel 2:1–10) is among the Old Testament canticles of the Liturgy of the Hours (Morning Prayer, Week II Wednesday in the Roman rite); confirm.
howItsDone: link to Saint Anne is a popular devotion (shared name in Latin, Anna); confirm it is fair to mention.
Hannah's name: commonly glossed as 'grace/favor'; confirm.
Audit (10% sample): cut the stock line 'a detail many readers love' and, in howItsDone, the unsourced claim that women ask Hannah's and Saint Anne's prayers.
